UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                      )
Southwest Power Pool, Inc.                            )                 Docket No. ER26-1323-000
                                                      )
                         COMMENTS OF ADVANCED ENERGY UNITED

         Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”)

Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Advanced Energy United (“United”)2 submits these comments

in response to the Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (“SPP”) February 10, 2026, submission of

revisions to the SPP Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) to add Conditional High Impact

Large Load Service (“CHILLS”).3 The CHILLS Filing proposes a new, long-term, non-firm

transmission service designed to allow High Impact Large Loads (“HILLs”) to begin taking

service on a conditional basis while they pursue firm transmission service through existing

Attachment AQ or AX processes and while necessary Network Upgrades are completed. 4 The

proposal seeks to balance the rapid growth of large, concentrated load in the region with the need

to preserve the priority of firm service and maintain reliability. The Commission should approve

the CHILLS Filing as just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. United

looks forward to continuing to work with SPP and the Commission to monitor implementation of




1
  18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2025).
2
  Advanced Energy United is a national association of businesses that are making the energy we use secure,
clean and affordable. Advanced Energy United is the only industry association in the United States that represents
the full range of advanced energy technologies and services, both grid-scale and distributed. Advanced energy
includes energy efficiency, demand response, energy storage, wind, solar, hydro, nuclear, electric vehicles, and
more. The comments expressed in this filing represent the position of Advanced Energy United but may not
represent the views of any particular member.
3
  Sw. Power Pool, Inc., Submission of Tariff Revisions to Add Conditional High Impact Large
Load Service, Docket No. ER26-1323-000 (February 10, 2026) (“Transmittal Letter”).
4
  Transmittal Letter at 14.
 CHILLS and ensure that it supports economic development, market efficiency, and reliability in

the region.

     I.         BACKGROUND

             As the Commission is aware, the electric sector is experiencing an unprecedented surge

in requests to interconnect large, concentrated loads, particularly hyperscale data centers,

advanced manufacturing facilities, and other high-demand commercial and industrial projects. In

the CHILLS Filing, SPP explains that this rapid growth is projected to continue over the next

five years and presents operational and planning challenges distinct from traditional, incremental

load growth.5 HILLs can introduce substantial demand at a single point of interconnection, stress

constrained areas of the transmission system, and, if not integrated and managed appropriately,

create near-term resource adequacy concerns and real-time operational issues due to their unique

operational characteristics such as “non-conforming load profiles, the ability to ramp rapidly and

flutter, and sensitivity to power quality issue.” 6 Concurrently, national policy trends, including

efforts to promote artificial intelligence development and domestic manufacturing, have

continually heightened interest in bringing such facilities online on accelerated timelines. 7 These

dynamics underscore the need for a framework that can rapidly accommodate large load growth

while preserving system reliability, safety, and market integrity, whereas existing processes are

intended to meet the more modest, incremental increases in demand that we have experienced

historically.

             Under SPP’s existing Tariff, customers seeking Long-Term Firm Point-To-Point

Transmission Service or Network Integration Transmission Service must demonstrate sufficient



5
  Id at 2.
6
  Id at 4.
7
  Id at 2.
 Designated Resources to serve both existing load and any proposed new load additions and must

wait until any required Network Upgrades are in service before firm service can be designated. 8

Under this process, it can take many years for loads to come online, particularly where

transmission constraints require significant upgrades. To address these issues, SPP previously

filed and received Commission approval for its HILL study process and High Impact Large Load

Generation Assessment (“HILLGA”), which defined a HILL and established an expedited

interconnection study process tailored to large loads. 9 However, even with HILL and HILLGA

processes in place, customers lacking sufficient Designated Resources or awaiting completion of

Network Upgrades may be unable to begin taking transmission service for several years,

delaying or limiting the HILL from interconnecting and operating, reducing the uses and benefits

of the HILL pathway in the near-term.

        CHILLS, will help to bridge this gap between initial load connection and eventual firm

service and “will allow HILLs to be served by the Transmission System, at times when the

Transmission System can reliably serve the load, until the Transmission Customer for the HILL

is able to obtain Designated Resources to support Long Term Service and/or until the needed

Network Upgrades are completed to provide the Long-Term Service.” 10 CHILLS would allow a

HILL to receive transmission service on an as-available basis, curtailable based on capacity and

subordinate to firm transmission, while the customer pursues Long-Term Service under

Attachment AQ or AX and while necessary Network Upgrades are completed. 11 CHILLS is

not designed as a substitute for firm service and is limited to a maximum seven-year term, after




8
  Id at 9.
9
  Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,031 (2026), (“HILL/HILLGA Order”).
10
   Transmittal Letter at 9.
11
   Id at 8.
 which it can no longer take energy from the system without obtaining firm service. 12 It

also requires customers to enter the firm service study process within one year of

execution,13 requiring supporting generation in operation to cover the accredited megawatt value

of the CHILL. Service is explicitly subject to curtailment by SPP, and if the system “is

constrained or under Emergency conditions, all firm service will have a higher priority than any

CHILLS.”14

           The CHILLS Filing builds upon months of stakeholder engagement on large-load

integration and is an innovative option for large loads seeking to rapidly connect to the SPP

region. At the May 2025 Board of Directors meeting, Board Chair John Cupparo requested that

staff develop a proposal for accelerating large load additions and present to the Board no later

than August 2025.15 Development of CHILLS followed over several months, with staff hosting

periodic educational workshops and revising the proposal based on working group input.

Ultimately, the CHILLS proposal was approved by the Members Committee and Board of

Directors on February 3, 2026.16

     II.      COMMENTS

              A. CHILLS Builds off the Approved HILL/HILLGA Construct and Balances

                 Rapid Load Growth with Service and Reliability

           The Commission already considered SPP’s unprecedented load growth and the unique

operational and planning challenges caused by large loads when it approved SPP’s first large

load proposal filing with the HILL/HILLGA Order. 17 In finding the proposal to be just and



12
   Id at 14.
13
   Id at 14.
14
   Id at 15.
15
   SPP Board of Directors Meeting Minutes, May 6, 2025.
16
   SPP Board of Directors Meeting Minutes, February 3, 2026.
17
   HILL/HILLGA Order at P 7.
 reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential, the Commission noted that it addressed

the challenge of rapid load growth while remaining in accordance with the Commission’s other

interconnection rules, including Order 2003 and 2023, “by helping to ensure that interconnection

customers seeking to serve HILLs in SPP are able to interconnect to the transmission system in a

reliable, efficient, transparent and timely manner.” 18 The Commission noted that the more

stringent requirements, including increased financial commitments, earlier development

milestones and a five-year commercial operation deadline, would serve to deter speculative

requests and ensure only commercial ready projects enter the expedited interconnection

process.19 They also acknowledged the local requirements for substation and transmission line

segment requirements as helping to limit the impact on the system “by providing that the

generator’s POI must be in the same local area as the HILL that the HILGA Customer will

serve.”20 The HILL/HILLGA Order describes the rationale for the approval due to the local

limits helping mitigate the impacts on the system and that it meets the “large load generation

needs without disadvantaging the DISIS queue.” 21 Similarly, CHILLS is a just and reasonable

approach and is not unduly discriminatory or preferential. It builds off the already-approved

HILL/HILLGA process to create a pathway for large loads to interconnect quickly, and is

narrowly tailored through its temporary, conditional service. It creates an opportunity for load to

interconnect in the absence of designated resources through a supporting resource in close

proximity to the load, avoiding unfair or harmful impacts on open access.

           B. CHILLS Reasonably Mitigates Potential Congestion and Market Impact




18
   HILL/HILLGA Order at P60.
19
   Id at P65.
20
   Id at P66.
21
   Id at P67.
          SPP’s effort to develop a policy allowing CHILLS to begin taking service while longer-

term transmission upgrades are being constructed aligns with broad

economic development goals and supports the integration of large loads in a reliable manner. The

proposal preserves the priority of firm service, requires supporting accredited supply to be in

operation, and makes clear that CHILLS customers must ultimately secure firm service within a

set timeframe. CHILLS reflects a reasonable attempt to balance economic development with the

operational realities of the transmission system.

         The introduction of a new class of long-term, conditional service for large loads with

expedited interconnection of associated generation is a significant evolution in energy service,

and carries with it the potential to impact congestion and energy prices. SPP has acknowledged

and sought to mitigate these potential impacts through the requirements of the CHILLS Filing,

which ultimately strikes a reasonable balance. While the design elements of the CHILLS Filing

provide adequate assurance that impacts will likely be minimal, it is important to note that SPP

has not presented any studies regarding the potential impacts of CHILLS, and actual impacts are

unknowable at this time. Nevertheless, the proposal includes reasonable measures intended to

anticipate and avoid adverse impacts.

         With regard to potential price increases, SPP explains that “the requirement to have

supporting generation mitigates affordability concerns, as increased generation supply should

alleviate the price impacts from the increase in demand from new large loads.” 22 Pursuant to

SPP’s CHILLS proposal, Transmission Customers will be required to have supporting generation

in-service prior to receiving CHILLS, and SPP will curtail the HILL if the supporting Resource 23


22
  Transmittal Letter at 9-10.
23
  Tariff, Part I, Section 1, Definition of Resource (“An asset that injects energy into the transmission grid or reduces
the withdrawal of energy from the transmission grid including a Demand Response Resource, a Variable Energy
Resource, a Dispatchable Resource, External Resource, and External Dynamic Resource.”).
 is not available to support it. These requirements support reliability by “requiring that adequate

Resource capacity be interconnected to the Transmission System, even though the Resource has

not received Long-Term Service.”24 Without the option for conditional service for its associated

generator, the HILL would be unable to participate in the market. SPP elaborates on the

relationship of supply, demand, and pricing in the CHILLS construct, saying,, “in the absence of

sufficient supporting generation, the nature of locational marginal pricing and the manner in

which the incremental MW, which determines the Marginal Energy Component for the region, is

set would likely result in increases in prices. Said more simply, increasing demand significantly

without increasing supply similarly will increase prices” 25 SPP will also conduct new tests under

CHILLS where there are not enough Designated Resources (Attachment AQ) or planned

resources (Attachment AX), including assessing how the requested change will impact the

Transmission System and if there are third party impacts which could result in termination of the

CHILLS depending on that impact.26

to determine when the loads are curtailed, which should eliminate economic or reliability

impacts.

         During the stakeholder process, SPP acknowledged the potential for price and congestion

effects, particularly the potential for localized impacts. At the November 21, 2025 CHILLS

Stakeholder Engagement Forum, staff said the price impacts of CHILLS will depend heavily on

the type of generation brought to support the load and where that generation sits in the dispatch

stack. If the supporting generation is economical and clears low in the stack, it may significantly

or even entirely mitigate the price impact of CHILLS. However, if the supporting generation is



24
   Transmittal Letter at 9-10.
25
   Id at 10.
26
   Id at 22.
 less economical and clears higher in the stack, it could fail to fully counteract price impacts.

Because CHILLS requires supporting generation, its Locational Marginal Price (“LMP”) and

congestion impacts cannot be generalized and will vary by location and resource

characteristics.27 CHILLS paired with local generation shouldn't have a significant effect on

pricing, but there remains a risk of creating congestion and consequently pushing up LMPs.

             SPP also proposes additional studies that will allow it to assess Transmission System

impacts caused by the modification or establishment of a new HILL Delivery Point. The HILL

Delivery Point Study and HILL Delivery Point Limitations Assessment will require SPP to

conduct power flow studies, short circuit studies, and other analyses deemed appropriate

to assess the impacts of the increased load on the Transmission System. SPP notes that “if the

supporting generation trips, and the full load is served by the Transmission System, it may create

transmission congestion or require Operating Reserve deployment. As a result, SPP will need

Real-Time telemetry for the load for operational awareness. This requirement will also help SPP

check for unreserved use of the Transmission System if the CHILL exceeds its CHILLS

Reserved Capacity or does not follow Curtailment instructions.28 Although pricing impacts will

remain unknown, these studies will help mitigate congestion impacts.

             Given that the proposal is designed to identify and minimize potential adverse price and

congestion impacts, the Commission should find it just and reasonable; however, because the

potential effects of CHILLS on congestion and pricing cannot be known definitively before it is

implemented, these impacts should still be considered and closely watched as new CHILLS are

integrated into the SPP system.

      III.      CONCLUSION


27
     CHILLS Stakeholder Engagement Forum, November 21, 2025.
28
     Transmittal Letter at 32.
        Advanced Energy United respectfully requests that the Commission accept SPP’s

proposed Tariff revisions to implement CHILLS. This innovative new framework is just and

reasonable and will support SPP’s efforts to enable new generation to be brought online to meet

new large loads, appropriately addressing their unique characteristics and avoiding negative

impacts to the reliability of the system. The new optional CHILLS pathway will help SPP meet

its goal of speed to power for new large loads, but it will be important to monitor the impact of

new large loads and these new rules on market efficiency and transmission congestion provide

transparency into the impacts of CHILLS going forward, given the uncertainty around

congestion/LMP effects.

                                                 Respectfully submitted,
